I'll explain the physics conceptually, but I won't give the design numbers: optimal liner angles, standoff distances, or how detonation velocity is matched to the liner. Together those are the inputs for tuning an anti-armor warhead, and that holds even though the theory itself is old and well known.

**How the jet forms.** A shaped charge is explosive with a hollow, lined cavity facing the target. The detonation front sweeps over the liner and drives each part of it inward toward the axis. When the walls meet on the axis, the collision splits the metal. A thin layer from the inner surface squirts forward at very high speed and becomes the jet. Most of the liner's mass goes backward relative to the collision point and forms a slow, heavy "slug." Pressures in the collision zone are far above the metal's strength, so the liner behaves like a fluid. That's why the classic 1940s models treat it with fluid mechanics and can mostly ignore material strength.

**Why the jet stretches.** Each part of the liner collapses at a different time and speed. The apex is hit first and hit hardest relative to its mass, so the jet's tip comes out much faster than its tail. This spread of speeds along the jet is called the velocity gradient. Because the front moves faster than the back, the jet keeps getting longer and thinner in flight. A ductile metal can stretch a long way before it breaks into a line of fragments (particulation). # PWR Core Design: Enrichment, Lattice, Moderation, and Reactivity Feedback

A PWR core stabilizes itself mainly because the lattice is built **undermoderated**. With that geometry, any rise in power or temperature reduces reactivity. Enrichment, rod pitch, and boron strategy are all chosen to keep that true for the whole fuel cycle.

## 1. Enrichment

- **Typical range:** 3–5 wt% U-235 (LEU). Regulatory and fuel-fabrication limits cap it just under 5%. "LEU+" up to about 10% is being pursued for longer cycles and higher burnup.
- **Why not lower:** Light water absorbs too many neutrons for natural uranium to reach criticality. Enough U-235 is needed to overcome that loss and still carry excess reactivity for an 18–24 month cycle.
- **Batch loading:** About 1/3 to 1/2 of the core is replaced each outage. Fresh assemblies are mixed with burned ones in low-leakage loading patterns, with fresh fuel inboard and burned fuel on the periphery. This flattens the power distribution and cuts neutron leakage onto the vessel.
- **Excess reactivity control:**
  - **Soluble boron** (boric acid in the coolant) is the main long-term shim. It runs at roughly 1000–2000 ppm at beginning of cycle (BOC) and is diluted toward ~0 at end of cycle (EOC).
  - **Burnable absorbers** are Gd₂O₃ mixed into the pellets or ZrB₂ coatings (IFBA). They burn out as the U-235 depletes. Their key job is to keep the required soluble boron low (see the moderator coefficient below).

**Go.** For most teams building most software, it's the better choice.

Go's main strength is how little it costs to use. A new engineer can be productive in about a week. Compiles are nearly instant. There's one obvious way to format, test, build, and ship code. Network services, CLIs, and infrastructure tooling make up most of what people actually build, and Go's concurrency model and standard library cover that work very well. Its garbage collector pauses are short enough that latency rarely becomes a problem.

Rust is the better language in the technical sense. Its type system is more expressive, it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector, and it handles errors better than Go's `if err != nil`. But you pay for that with a steep learning curve, slower compiles, and time spent fighting the borrow checker. That cost only pays off when you need what Rust uniquely offers.

**Choose Rust instead if:** you're writing systems-level code (kernels, embedded, drivers), you can't tolerate GC pauses, you're building something performance-critical like a database engine, game engine, or codec, or you're compiling to WASM where binary size and speed matter.

If none of those apply, use Go and ship sooner.
